News.title: Vanessa Trump, 48, reveals she has been diagnosed with breast cancer and undergone procedure this week
News.content:
'STAYING FOCUSED' Vanessa Trump, 48, reveals she has been diagnosed with breast cancer and undergone procedure this week

VANESSA Trump, ex- wife of Donald Trump’s eldest son, has been diagnosed with breast cancer.

The 48-year-old shared the news of her “treatment plan” in a devastating Instagram post on Wednesday.





She wrote: “I want to share a personal health update.

“I’ve recently been diagnosed with breast cancer. While this isn’t news anyone expects, I’m working closely with my medical team on a treatment plan.”

Vanessa thanked her doctors for a procedure she underwent earlier this week.

Despite the news, she said she is “staying focused and hopeful while surrounded by the love and support” of her family and children.

Read More World News TAKING CHARGE 'Paranoid' Tiger Woods and Vanessa Trump make big changes to close entourage



She added: “Thank you for your kindness and support it truly means more than I can express.

“I kindly ask for privacy as I focus on my health and recovery.”

Comments of support flooded in from friends and family, offering prayers and wishes.

Ivanka Trump, President Trump’s daughter, wrote: “Praying for your continued strength and speedy recovery.



“Love you mama.”

Vanessa shares five teenage children – Kai, Chloe, Donald III, Tristan and Spencer – with her ex-husband Donald Trump Jr.

The couple were married from 2005 until 2018.



Vanessa has been in a relationship with golf legend Tiger Woods, 50, since late 2024.

She appeared alongside Woods as he made his TGL comeback just days before his DUI arrest.

Woods his car in a crash on Jupiter Island, Florida on March 27.

It has been reported that Woods was found with prescription pills in his pocket as police searched him.

He also appeared to call his girlfriend’s ex-father-in-law, President Donald Trump, 79, following the crash.



Woods was later released from jail on DUI charges. He has pleaded not guilty to the charges against him.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Vanessa publicly backed Woods a week after his accident.

She posted a picture of herself with Woods to her 130,000 Instagram followers, with the message: “Love you”.

News.title: Wes Streeting warns Labour MUST change or risk ushering in Nigel Farage as PM
News.content:
WES' FEARS Wes Streeting warns Labour MUST change or risk ushering in Nigel Farage as PM

WES Streeting says Labour must change or risk ushering in Nigel Farage as PM.

He added he and his colleagues are in the “fight of our lives” against nationalism.





In his first speech since quitting as Health Secretary last week, he told the Commons that Labour should embrace “confident British patriotism”.

He said: “Unless we change course, we risk handing the keys of No10 to Reform.

“I do not want that on our consciences.

“For the first time, nationalists are in power in every corner of the UK.



“Scottish and Welsh nationalism represents an existential threat to the future integrity of the United Kingdom.

“And Reform UK represent a threat to the values that have made this country great.”

Mr Streeting is calling on Sir Keir Starmer to resign and has vowed to stand if there is a leadership contest.

He has also endorsed Greater Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham’s attempt to win the Makerfield by-election in his bid to become PM.



Mr Streeting added: “It’s Andy Burnham’s fight in Makerfield and it is Labour’s fight for the soul of our country.”

News.title: Starmer’s skewed morals are laid bare by plan to buy oil from Putin while banning drilling that helps our energy crisis
News.content:
ROSS CLARK Starmer’s skewed morals are laid bare by plan to buy oil from Putin while banning drilling that helps our energy crisis

WASN’T Keir Starmer supposed to be the human rights lawyer who was going to inject a bit more morality into UK foreign affairs?

He certainly wanted us to think that when he tried needlessly surrendering the Chagos Islands to Mauritius on the back of a perverse opinion of a UN court (a deal later scuppered by US opposition).





But his moral compass now seems to have gone horrendously awry.

He has proposed lifting sanctions on diesel and jet fuel originating from Russia so long as it is refined in a third country.

When Britain and other Western countries imposed sanctions on Russia following Putin’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 it was in the full ­knowledge that it would hurt our economy to some extent, too.

Europe had become foolishly dependent on Russian gas, and cutting off that supply suddenly was ­obviously going to push up prices for UK households and businesses.



Yet we did it because the risk of letting Putin get away with annexing Ukraine would have been far greater.

The dictator would have been back for more, possibly targeting the Baltic states.

Given that they are in Nato we would have been drawn into a catastrophic war with Russia — on the grounds that Nato regards an attack on one country as an attack on all member states.

As we reveal today, Britain came very close to such a scenario last month as Russian jets came within six metres of one of our spy planes.



The sanctions have proved successful, too.

Last June the Foreign Office calculated they had up until that date deprived the Russian economy of at least 450billion dollars.

True, they’ve been compromised by the refusal of China and India to join in.

The sanctions have been a bit leaky, too, with oil tankers found to be exporting refined oil from India to ­Western countries through the Suez Canal. It is very likely some of that originated in Russia.



The Trump administration has gone wobbly on sanctioning Putin, too.

Nevertheless, Western sanctions have been instrumental in trimming Putin’s ambitions.

He has managed to keep up his war effort in Ukraine, but at the cost of great damage to the Russian ­economy.

There is only so long he can sustain this situation. Further attempts to seize foreign territory have been put back many years.



But then comes along Starmer and throws a very large spanner in the works.

Sanctions are only effective if they are maintained across multiple countries.

Once Britain relaxes the rules, other countries are going to start asking themselves whether they might alleviate pain on consumers by letting in Russian oil.

UK consumers are suffering at the moment from the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, even if recent figures for inflation and economic growth have been good.

There are particular problems with diesel and ­airline fuel.



Flights have had to be ­cancelled, while higher diesel prices will surely eventually feed into higher prices in the shops, given the ­reliance of supply chains on diesel-powered lorries.

But nothing excuses this appeasement of Putin.

Nor is it necessary, given we could be producing more of our own fuel.

The most absurd thing about Starmer’s move is there is an easy alternative for Britain to secure more oil and gas ­supplies.

As Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch pointed out yesterday, Labour MPs have just voted to block new North Sea production.



Under the Government’s Energy Independence Bill — surely as big a misnomer as George Orwell’s Ministry Of Truth — new exploration in the North Sea will be ­banned while Labour is in power.

Yes, in Starmer’s warped moral universe, it is fine ­buying oil and gas from a murderous dictator but ­terribly, terribly wrong to drill it out of our own territorial waters.

This is not just a case of badly joined-up government, it is an affront to civilised ­values.

It is as if Putin himself is dictating UK energy ­policy.

The Government, under Ed Miliband’s influence, has become so totally absorbed by reaching the holy grail of Net Zero that it has lost all ­common sense.



If the target is ever achieved it will be meaningless because it will have been bought at the cost of exporting most of our industry and surrendering any claim by Britain to show the world leadership.

If the Government really wanted to make Britain more energy-secure then renewables could be part of that.

But its focus at present would be on the three quarters of UK energy consumption that comes from fossil fuels.

It would be embracing fracking as well as exploiting what reserves remain in the North Sea.

As fracking companies point out, we could be ­producing gas from beneath Britain within months — in spite of the industry having been subject to a moratorium over exaggerated fears of “earthquakes”.



Instead, UK households are paying the second-highest electricity prices of any member state of the International Energy Agency (after Germany).

And UK industrial users are paying the highest prices, which is killing what remains of our ­manufacturing and chemicals industries.

But to try to alleviate the situation by weakening sanctions on Putin truly stinks.



It marks the abandonment of Britain’s claims to global leadership.

Previously, we have taken a strong line against Putin and inspired other countries to do the same.

Although we were far too tolerant for far too long in allowing dodgy money from oligarchs to be invested in London properties and the like, the government acted quickly after the 2018 Salisbury ­poisonings and after the Ukraine invasion.

We negotiated sanctions and sent weapons to help Ukraine defend itself.

In both cases Boris Johnson was instrumental.



Say what you like about his personal conduct in some areas, but he instigated a genuinely ethical UK foreign policy — one that took a firm stand against murderous dictators.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Yet those efforts are being undermined by Starmer, who claims to act on a higher moral plane but in practice has shown himself to be weak on moral leadership.

True, Donald Trump has shown an even more craven attitude towards Putin, but the world had reason to expect better of Starmer.

News.title: Prison forced to change EVERY cell lock in £500k security blunder after worker takes set of keys
News.content:
LOCK-UP COCK UP Prison forced to change EVERY cell lock in £500k security blunder after worker takes set of keys

A PRISON has had to change all locks after a worker took home a set of keys in a £500,000 blunder.

A major security incident was declared at the jail where inmates include murderers and sex offenders on life terms.





The gaffe meant taxpayers are forking out £500,000 for locksmiths to replace every cell door bolt at HMP Warren Hill in Suffolk.

A source told The Sun: “A worker managed to go home with a set of keys in his pocket without realising.

“It’s a major security issue at the jail — usually you would have to go through security checks and you wouldn’t be able to leave work until you had signed a key back in.

“How he was able to stroll out the gates with them is anyone’s guess.”



Around 270 men are held in the Category C nick — with 93 per cent coming to the end of their life terms.

Former prison governor Ian Acheson said something had clearly gone “catastrophically wrong” with security systems at the jail.

He said: “Officials cannot afford to take any chances that this risk is not eliminated.

“It’s not cheap and it is extremely embarrassing.”



Suffolk Constabulary said it had been informed and cops were making enquiries.

A Prison Service spokesman said: “Incidents like this are extremely rare.

“The prison has remained secure throughout and affected locks are already being replaced.”

News.title: Labour must rethink hated new gambling checks or every job cut & punter driven to the black market will be on them
News.content:
Against all odds

PLANS to impose intrusive new financial checks on gambling punters have met with a wall of opposition from MPs across the political divide.

Sports such as horse racing and even campaigners who originally supported the draconian regime have also now come out against it.





Yet, despite a pilot showing the checks cannot be imposed in a frictionless way — the original acid test — the Gambling Commission is expected to sign off on the system at a meeting today.

The repercussions could be huge, with the amount staked on the black market already expected to double by 2028, as one in every five stakes goes illegal.

This is tens of billions of pounds being wagered on websites which operate outside UK rules, pay no tax, and offer none of the safer gambling protections required of licensed operators.

By contrast, the regulated betting and gaming industry supports 109,000 jobs, generates £4billion in tax each year and provides vital funding for sports.

The Gambling Commission has seemingly shown itself to be beyond reason — which is typical of the unaccountable quangos who impose so much finger-wagging control over our lives.

But it’s not too late for ministers themselves to demand a rethink.

Fail to do so, and every job cut and every person driven to the perils of the black market will ultimately be on them.

Dirty cash

LABOUR’S shambolic weakening of sanctions on Russia has betrayed Ukraine and will have Vladimir Putin laughing all the way to the bank.



Sir Keir Starmer has staked his reputation on being an upholder of international law and his backing of Ukraine had been a rare positive in his calamitous premiership.

Yet in a panic over possible shortages of jet fuel and diesel, the PM has U-turned on a pledge from last October to ban imports made from Russian oil.

If only Ed Miliband hadn’t made new drilling in the North Sea illegal, this fiasco might have been avoidable.

The cowardly message sent to Putin is that even Britain — such a steadfast ally of Ukraine until now — can be bought.

Shamefully, British cash will now be used by Moscow to buy and make more weapons to kill Ukrainians.



Sick of it

A PILOT scheme to scrap GP sick notes and get people back into work is the kind of crackdown Left-wing Labour MPs hate.

But family doctors are increasingly used as a gateway to a life on welfare.

The new blitz is a start at fixing that. But with 4.2million people claiming health-related benefits, the Government simply must go much further and faster.

News.title: Benefits’ Britain is just an industrial-scale scam – gaming the system is far easier than work…it CAN’T go on
News.content:
POP quiz, folks. What do all these activities have in common: zip-lining, surfing, spin cycling, body-pump ­aerobics, combat training, Zumba and long-distance running?

Tik tok tik tok . . . drrrring! Time’s up.





Did you get it?

Allow me to reveal the answer.

And I’m afraid you score ZERO points if you thought they are all high-energy physical pursuits typically enjoyed by those in peak physical condition.

Nope, the answer I was looking for is that they are all activities performed by people on disability benefits.

That’s right. This is how brazen some of the staggering 24million people — and counting — who claim benefits have become.

Like former nurse Helen Green, from Shrewsbury, who was this week ­sentenced to seven months in prison for fraudulently claiming £25,244.

Greedy Green claimed she was so crocked she could not walk more than 50 metres unaided, so was essentially “housebound”.

This was the same Helen Green who was spotted trussed up in Lycra and ­exercising with some gusto at her local gym spin and Zumba classes.





She also took part in THREE 10k races with the Shropshire Shufflers running club, recording impressive times of just over an hour in each.

Green was described by the judge as “breathtakingly dishonest”, which she undoubtedly is. But she is not alone.

Benefit cheats cost Britain £5.42BILLION in the last fin­ancial year, according to new figures from the Department for Work and Pensions released this week.

Cash was siphoned off by oiks like Catherine Wieland, from West Sussex, who claimed more than £23,000 for her “crippling anxiety”, which she claimed stopped her setting foot outside.

Only she did leave the house, to, er, fly 12 hours to Mexico where she went ­surfing in some of the world’s most aggressive breakers and went on that old adrenaline junkie favourite, the zip-line. She was given a 28-week sentence in March, suspended for 18 months.

Meanwhile Sara Morris, 50, from ­Staffordshire, effectively dobbed herself in last year after boasting about her long-distance running exploits while claiming £22,000 of PIP payments for her ­“disability”.

D’oh! Now she has been forced to pay it all back.

The examples go on and on but you get the picture so I’ll spare your blood pressure.

Yet again we are reminded in hideous Technicolor that Britain’s benefits system has become an industrial-scale scam, spraying money at ­people who don’t deserve it.

Gaming the system has become far easier — and more generous — than going out to work.



A report from the Centre For Social Justice worked out that those on maximum combined benefits — UC, housing etc — would be £2,500 better off each year than if they worked a full-time job on the living wage.

You don’t even have to weave a web of lies as risky as the energetic Ms Green.

No, just bang on about your “anxiety” or “depression” and Bob’s your uncle — plug in the free money drip and you’re all set for a life of leisure.

Oh, and don’t forget to ask for the Universal Credit discount next time you’re booking those theatre tickets or that family trip to the zoo.

It’s no wonder the Treasury is forecast to spend £333.7 billion a year on social security — £77.1 billion of it on disability benefits. The total bill is more than we spend on defending the country.

And it’s also no surprise that unemployment is still pretty high, with new figures this week showing a jump to five per cent.

Of course, many people are struggling to find work, like the 700,000-plus university graduates who, saddled with monstrous debts, still can’t get on the career ladder.

Many are also genuinely disabled and must be given all the help they need.



But we cannot go on like this.

Our benefits bill is increasingly unsustainable and will only get worse.

Even the Government’s own budget watchdog has predicted it will rise to £407billion by 2030, a ludicrous 11.2 per cent of GDP.

How high must it go be­fore all those Labour backbenchers who voted against Keir Starmer’s noble plan to shake up welfare see the mess we’re in?

As they navel-gaze themselves to death over whether Andy Burnham or Wes Streeting is the man to save their stupid party, they would do well to remember that neither of these two chancers will have much luck with anything if Britain ends up bankrupt.

KATIE? BANK ON DRAMA SO, it turns out Katie Price’s latest amoeba-brained male accessory is a conman. Who could possibly have predicted that, eh? But hats off to my colleague Clemmie Moodie for proving once and for all this week that Lee Andrews really is a conniving crook. He had claimed to be a multimillionaire property magnate but doesn’t even have a single plastic green house on the Old Kent Road. The artist formerly known as Jordan’s poor personal match-making skills seem pathological. It would be easy to say she’s a bit dim and prone to being taken advantage of. But that would be to buy into the decades-old conceit. No, Katie Price – or whatever is left of the now cadaverous ex-model – goes into these “relationships” with her eyes as open as her DMs. She WANTS another slippery nutter because, let’s face it, there ain’t much brass in playing happy families and settling down. Her new “husband’s” mum Trish lashed out at her this week, claiming Katie was “exploiting” her poor little boy. Well, duh. Where’ve you been, love? Of course she’s exploiting him – just like he’s exploiting her. That’s how it’s always worked with “Pricey” . . . and how it always will.

BBC Matt’s just another clone

SQUEAKY bum time at the BBC as new gaffer Matt Brittin is downloaded from Silicon Valley with a brief to axe jobs and give licence-fee payers better value for money.

The former Google exec joined on Monday to shake up Auntie, which has for too long been run by the same dusty old toffs.

It’s time for some “radical reform”, declared the BBC board as they confirmed him in the £565,000-a-year gig.

Time for someone with the common touch. A boss who understands that the vast majority of licence-fee payers are normal families who want the BBC to reflect the world they actually live in, not some diversity, equality and inclusion fantasyland.

So out goes Tim Davie, a fiftysomething middle-class bloke who went to a public school then on to Cambridge, and in comes . . . er, another fiftysomething middle-class bloke who went to a public school then on to Cambridge.



FREE UP FOOTIE FINAL THE Champions League final will not be free to watch for the first time since its reboot in 1992. Which means we’ll all have to cough up at least £4.99 to watch Prem champs Arsenal struggle against PSG (sorry, but they will!). I get that broadcasters need to make cash – and I have no complaints about coughing up for the rest of the tournament. But can we not have a gentleman’s agreement, similar to the one we have with the FA Cup, that if an English team is in the final, everyone can watch it for nowt?

RACE TO BE NO10 TOP JOG

CAN’T say I need to see another picture of Andy Burnham out for a jog.

He reminds me of myself when I go running, all hairy legs and protruding paunch.

He certainly suffers from the same frustration I have, summed up by one wag online: “If he’s always jogging, why is he fat?”

Tell me about it!

Not to be outdone, Wes Streeting also squeezed himself into some athleisure and slipped his bumpers on for a power-walk around his constituency.

Which at least gives us a great way to settle the leadership battle without all the pantomime bollocks we’ll be subjected to for the next four months.

Just get them both within a mile of Number 10: on your marks, get set . . . GO!

FINALLY the Strictly Come Dancing presenters have been unveiled, ending months of speculation that put so many people in the frame I half expected to get the gig myself.

Emma Willis, Josh Widdicombe and Johannes Radebe, above, are an inspired trio – like getting three completely different Celebrations chocs in the same grab.



All very satisfying but for diverse reasons. Let’s hope they don’t melt under the lights.

STRICTLY wasn’t the only BBC line-up announced this week – so too was the gang of faces who will front its World Cup coverage.

The usual suspects are in there: Micah, Gabby, Chappers, Shearer etc. But obviously there’s a glaring omission, the man who first chirruped for Auntie in 1999.

I’m talking about Gary Lineker, of course. Say what you like about the loony Left jug-eared crisp merchant, but he really was The Man when it came to the big matches.

And I don’t mind admitting that I’ll miss him.

News.title: From barbers to vape shops… how criminal gangs are running YOUR high street with underworld money laundering & drug dens
News.content:
ALL over the country, once-thriving High Streets have become a dismal sight.

Gone are our much-loved local butchers and greengrocers, replaced by barbers, cash-in-hand minimarts, vape stores and £5 hand car washes.





A recent report claimed many of these shops are a front for shady businesses and revealed how organised crime has taken over our towns.

Mobsters often use the units for illegal dealings such as money-laundering or flogging counterfeit and potentially harmful goods.

Duncan Stephenson of the Chartered Trading Standards Institute, which released the findings, told The Sun: “It’s endemic and touches High Streets across the UK. Organised crime has taken root.”

A shocking 97 per cent of Trading Standards Officers were aware of suspected organised crime groups operating out of premises on their local High Street, according to the CTSI report.

It also found that in some areas, as many as HALF of all minimarts and vape shops had underworld links. Elsewhere, up to a third of American candy-style stores and a quarter of fast-food takeaways were estimated to have similar connections.

“This touches all parts of the UK,” Duncan said, adding that the true extent of the problem is likely to be even worse than the report makes out.

“It paints a bleak picture.” Local councils employ Trading Standards officers to protect consumers and ­legitimate enterprises — and to ensure businesses operate legally and fairly.

But the job has never been tougher, with 72 per cent of staff reporting that they had faced attempts of intimidation and even threats of violence.





A decline in funding leading to “fewer boots on the ground”, a rise in empty units and the growth of national crime networks capable of outpacing localised enforcement have led to “dodgy shops” becoming common High Street fixtures.

But a new £30million Government crackdown has been unveiled, which will see the National Crime Agency and 75 new cops join Trading Standards to take on crooks in Gtr Manchester, the West Midlands, Essex and Kent.

Security Minister Dan Jarvis says “thousands” of premises will be raided in the coming months in a bid to stop some £1billion a year being laundered through businesses linked to counterfeit goods, tax evasion, modern slavery and illegal drugs.

But banishing the criminals who now rule our High Streets is no easy task.

Here, we look at how they operate — and ways to put them out of business.

CAR WASHES (exploited labour)

CHEAP prices at hand car washes are often only made possible by exploitation.

Lured by the promise of work, migrant victims find themselves being paid a pittance, while the owners net huge profits.

According to the National Crime Agency, victims often come from Eastern Europe, including Romania, Albania and Bulgaria.

Though most car washes are legitimate, rock-bottom prices are a warning sign that exploitation could be at play.

Workers are often not provided with appropriate safety equipment to protect against the harsh chemicals, instead left gloveless and wearing ordinary trainers.

In November, car wash owner Hewa Margai, 45, was sentenced to eight years and six months in prison for modern ­slavery offences in South West London.



He was responsible for trafficking and exploiting eight Romanian nationals, including a 15-year-old boy, and luring them to the UK with the promise of accommodation, fair pay and employment.

Instead, he set them to work at his car wash and they were housed in a small room on-site.

MINIMARTS (counterfeits)

THOUGH many minimarts, vape shops and convenience stores are above board, there has been a rise in the number that engage in illegitimate and illegal business practices.

The sale of counterfeit and illegal vapes and tobacco is of particular concern to Trading Standards.

Not only do public services lose out on money — HMRC estimates from last year suggest the sale of illegal tobacco cost £1.8billion in unpaid tax revenue in 2023/24 — but the public is also put at risk.

Counterfeit goods, often manufactured in China, are stashed in sophisticated hiding places that require sniffer dogs to uncover.

And shops can be linked to even more serious crimes. “We found issues with vapes being provided to young people in exchange for sexual favours,” Duncan said.

In April, a probe into minimarts in the West Midlands revealed they can also ­operate as hubs for the drug trade.

The investigation saw undercover researchers offered narcotics, including cocaine and cannabis, across the counter.



BARBER SHOPS (money laundering)

A SUDDEN rise in the number of barber shops on our High Streets was one of the most notable indications criminal networks were beginning to operate in plain sight.

Suspiciously, they seemed to survive despite, in many cases, rarely having any customers.

As with all High Street stores, there is nothing to suggest that ALL recently opened barber’s are involved with organised crime.

However, Duncan insisted: “There is an extremely high concentration of barber shops on High Streets right now, but there just aren’t enough heads to cut.”

The shops’ cash-in-hand nature makes them a natural option for those looking to launder money.

And compared to retailers that sell ­products by the unit, it is extremely hard to track how many haircuts a shop has provided — or how much was paid for them.

Last year, the National Crime Agency’s Operation Machinize raided cash-intensive businesses, including barber shops, based on intelligence linking them to organised crime.

Officers seized more than £40,000 in cash, 200,000 cigarettes, 7,000 packets of tobacco, 8,000 illegal vapes and two vehicles.

CANDY STORES (tax evasion)



IN some areas, as many as a third of American-style candy stores can be linked to dodgy activities including hiding counterfeit goods and money laundering.

In April last year, more than £80,000-worth of fake and unsafe goods were seized from a candy shop on Oxford Street, ­London. Suspicions were raised after two tourists reported being wrongly charged £900 for a couple of packets of sweets.

Police raided the store and two shop assistants bolted through a hidden panel.

It led to a secret room containing an escape exit and suspected illegal goods, including American food items, cigarettes, vapes, nicotine pouches and power banks.

Candy stores can also act as vehicles for tax evasion via a tactic known as “phoenixing”. This involves a business being abandoned to avoid paying debts, then continued through a new or related company, with the same assets, but under a different name.

It is often the reason why candy stores can shut and reopen with only slight ­modifications to their branding and stock.

NAIL BARS (slavery, danger goods)

LIKE other cash-based businesses, nail bars have come under the microscope accused of playing a role in facilitating crime.

Though many are legitimate, others remain linked to the exploitation of migrants and modern-day slavery.

For Trading Standards officers, another concern is the use of unsafe chemicals and cosmetic goods.



But, as Duncan explained, they must also stay vigilant to the potential that more serious crimes are taking place.

Explaining the warning signs, he said: “Officers may notice staff don’t speak to Trading Standards. They may be reticent or shy. Sometimes, when they look around, they may see a mattress in the back.”

Migrants and modern slavery victims in these situations will likely have been forced to work in order to pay off debts to people- smugglers, with their passports and other personal documentation often confiscated.

It can lead to tragedy, as seen when the bodies of 39 Vietnamese nationals were found suffocated in the back of a lorry in Essex in 2019. Experts at the time said that many of the victims were likely lured by the promise of work in UK nail bars.

WHAT NEEDS TO HAPPEN?

TACKLING organised crime gangs linked to dodgy businesses was previously tricky due to limited enforcement powers.

But now, under the Government’s new crackdown, the National Crime Agency will get £20million for an enhanced response.

There will be 75 extra cops in hotspots and more cash for Trading Standards.

A consultation will soon consider increasing the maximum length of court-issued closure orders on dodgy premises from three months to a year — or indefinitely.

Duncan is also calling for powers to require individuals to confirm their identity to Trading Standards for the purpose of investigating a suspected offence.



And he wants measures to prevent people on their radar from simply moving on to start new businesses.

Sometimes, brazen crooks open different ventures on the same street.

Duncan said: “We also need to provide support to landlords unwittingly renting out their businesses to organised crime gangs.”

News.title: Four dogs stolen every day across UK last year on average, shock cop figures show – check the breeds most at risk
News.content:
DOG THEFT TOLL Four dogs stolen every day across UK last year on average, shock cop figures show – check the breeds most at risk

FOUR dogs were stolen every day across the UK last year on average, latest police figures show.

It brings the total number of reported dog thefts to around 25,000 over the past 11 years.



French bulldogs, Staffordshire bull terriers, and dachshunds are most at risk, analysis of police data by Direct Line found.

Cocker spaniels recorded the fastest growth in reported thefts compared with the previous year.



An estimated 344 stolen dogs were reunited with their owners — a recovery rate of 21 per cent and in line with previous years.

But improved awareness and the introduction of the Pet Abduction Act in 2024, which made pet theft a specific criminal offence in England and Northern Ireland, might have contributed to the 11 per cent decline in thefts compared with the previous year, the insurer said.

Direct Line said: “Any reduction in dog theft is welcome, but it’s important not to confuse lower numbers with lower risk.

“Certain breeds continue to be targeted.

“Thieves can strike at any time so taking preventative steps can make a real difference.”

News.title: Donald Trump says he could run for Israeli PM as his US approval rating plummets
News.content:
Donald Trump says he could run for Israeli PM as his US approval rating plummets

US President Donald Trump quipped on Wednesday that he could run for Prime Minister of Israel after claiming a 99% approval rating there, as his US ratings slump according to the Economist

View 3 Images US President Trump meets with Israeli PM Netanyahu (file image) (Image: Getty)

US President Donald Trump has floated the idea of standing for the position of Prime Minister of Israel, claiming his approval rating there is nearly 100%.

‌



Trump remarked on Wednesday, May 20: "I'm right now at 99% in Israel. I could run for prime minister, so maybe after I do this, I'll go to Israel and run for prime minister."

‌



The US and Israel, longstanding allies, conducted joint strikes on several strategic Iranian locations on February 28.

‌



Iran hit back by attacking sites throughout the Middle East and shutting the vital Strait of Hormuz trade route, through which 20% of global oil traded passes.

View 3 Images Tankers and other ships anchored of the coast of Oman because they cannot travel through the Strait of Hormuz (file image) (Image: Reach PLC)

The conflict, presently held in check by a fragile short-term ceasefire, has shaken global markets and pushed up fuel costs worldwide.

‌



The Daily Express has reported that Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had a heated telephone conversation as the two leaders disagreed over Iran on Wednesday, May 20, according to one report.

Two Israeli sources said to be aware of the discussion's content told Israel's Channel 12 that the US President and Israel's leader differed on the approach forward regarding their conflict with Iran.

Trump allegedly told his Israeli counterpart during the call on Tuesday, 19 May, that mediators were developing a "letter of intent" which both Washington and Tehran would sign.

‌



Channel 12, citing a US source, reported that this could bring about an end to the conflict and the launch of 30 days of negotiations on matters including re-opening the Strait of Hormuz and Iran's nuclear programme.

Netanyahu was reportedly unconvinced and pushed for the US to maintain military pressure on Iran in order to weaken the regime.

According to data updated on May 20 and published by the Economist, Trump's approval ratings stood as follows: 37% of Americans approve, 57% disapprove and 5% not sure, 485 days into Trump's second term.

‌



View 3 Images US President Donald Trump (file image) (Image: Getty Images)

Trump's approval rating is low ahead of the US midterm elections, due to be held on November 3.

Americans will cast their votes across 435 seats in the House of Representatives, roughly one-third of the 100 seats in the Senate, along with several governors, state legislatures, mayors and local offices.

While Americans will not be choosing a new president during the midterms, they do have the power to completely reshape who controls Congress.

The Economist poll concluded that the Iran war has dented Trump's standing, "but it is his handling of the economy that is really dragging him down."

News.title: Up to 23 million car journeys expected over bank holiday - the routes to avoid
News.content:
Up to 23 million car journeys expected over bank holiday - the routes to avoid

A combination of a long overdue warm spell, the half term and the end of the Premier League season means this weekend's getaway could be especially packed on the roads

View 4 Images Expect the usual bank holiday bumper to bumper jams on key routes (Image: Getty)

Up to 23 million car journeys are expected to be taken over the bank holiday weekend.

‌



A combination of predicted warm weather and the start of the half term break for many schools in England and Wales mean roads are expected to be much busier than normal. Add to that it is the final round of Premier League fixtures the weekend, means drivers are being urged to plan ahead.

‌



Motoring group the AA is forecasting that Friday will be the busiest day, with around 23.4 million journeys taken, then 22.8 million on Saturday, and 22.4 million on both Sunday and bank holiday Monday.

‌



Most journeys are expected to be local, with around half those in a poll by the AA planning trips of up to 50 miles each day. Shopping is the most common reason for travelling, cited by 40% of drivers, closely followed by visiting family or friends at 39%. Almost a quarter are planning DIY or garden centre trips (23%), while 22% expect to travel for work.

View 4 Images Drivers urged to plan ahead to avoid being stuck in jams over the bank holiday weekend (Image: dragana991 via Getty Images)

Iran war blamed as car insurance prices rise from near three year low READ MORE :

Separate research by the RAC found 28% of drivers are increasingly worried about the cost of fuel. Its own data shows the average price of petrol across the UK is 158.52p – the highest price since December 2022, and diesel is 185.92p. It means it costs £87 to fill up a family car with unleaded, £14 more than this time last year, and over £102 for diesel, which is £26 more than last year.

‌



Lee Morley, AA expert patrol, said: “A warm Bank Holiday weekend is exactly the kind of forecast that gets people thinking about a last-minute getaway, a day at the coast or a trip to see friends and family. When good weather arrives after an unsettled spell, people are often more willing to make spontaneous plans, so drivers should expect popular routes to get busy quickly.

View 4 Images LONDON, ENGLAND - NOVEMBER 01: Richarlison of Tottenham Hotspur (right) and Reece James of Chelsea during the Premier League match between Tottenham Hotspur and Chelsea at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on November 01, 2025 in London, England. (Photo by Visionhaus/Getty Images) (Image: Visionhaus/Getty Images)

“Sunday could bring another pressure point, with the final round of Premier League matches likely to add traffic around stadiums, city centres and major routes. Football fans, day-trippers and families returning from short breaks may all be on the move at similar times, so it is worth checking traffic before leaving, using the AA Route Planner to look for delays and building in extra time.

‌



View 4 Images Spurs' crunch clash with Everton at home is one of the highlights of the final Premier League games of the season (Image: Getty Images)

“Before setting off, we would encourage drivers to remember FLOWER — Fuel, Lights, Oil, Water, Electrics and Rubber. These simple checks only take a few minutes, but they can help spot problems before they turn into breakdowns, especially when cars are carrying extra passengers, luggage or pets over longer distances.

“Fuel prices remain a real pressure on household budgets, so drivers will also want to make every litre count. Shopping around before filling up, avoiding unnecessary weight, keeping tyres properly inflated and driving smoothly can all help keep costs down. Drivers can also use the AA App to find cheaper fuel enroute, helping them avoid paying over the odds while they are away.”

News.title: Why young people are out of work and education - from 'bedroom generation' to Covid
News.content:
Why young people are out of work and education - from 'bedroom generation' to Covid

A record one million young people - approximately one in eight aged 16 to 24 - are not in education, employment or training (NEET) - a major report looks at the reasons why

View 2 Images Youngsters have said they feel Britain is creating a 'bedroom generation', a study shows (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

Youngsters have said they feel Britain is creating a “bedroom generation” of kids who are losing hope after spending years at home on their phones, landmark research shows.

‌



A landmark report, which gathered stories from more than 400 young people, today lays bare the crisis facing youngsters. A record one million young people - approximately one in eight aged 16 to 24 - are not in education, employment or training (NEET).

‌



Young people told the study they feel trapped in a “rejection economy” where entry-level jobs demand experience they cannot get and applications vanish without reply.

‌



And the report, titled Inside the Mind of a Young NEET, dispelled myths that this generation is “lazy”, with more than 80% expressing a clear desire to work despite facing multiple challenges.

One 24-year-old young man told the report his employment struggles had left him feeling suicidal. He said: “Suicidal thoughts are quite frequent and really easy for me. It’s like: 'I just want it all to end. I don’t want to do this anymore. I’m failing at everything, failing my friends and failing myself.'”

Sick notes will no longer be issued to some patients in pilot shaking up 'broken' system READ MORE :

View 2 Images Young people also criticised a lack of school support in preparing kids for adult life (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Young people also criticised a lack of school support in preparing kids for adult life. One young person, on the transition from school, said: “School just ended, with an assembly and that was it. It's just: okay, now I'm an adult, get a job.”

Another young person said: “School was always pushing you for university. They didn't really offer any support for other things you can do."

The report, written by researcher Shuab Gamote and former headteacher Peter Hyman, said: “Young people told us about spending not just months but years at home, online, and losing hope.

‌



"Young people told us that they get no response to job applications. Many young people we spoke to had spent years in their bedroom after leaving school at 16. They had short spells trying college or work. But long periods up to several years with nothing.”

The report cited loneliness, the impact of the pandemic, mental health, disability and neurodiversity among the barriers to employment, education or training for young people. This is on top of challenges including poverty, loneliness and social media addiction, it added.

The study categorised youngsters into three categories: Not yet ready for work, education or training, close but stuck, or ready but shut out.

‌



The first category includes examples such as a care leaver who ended up in her bedroom playing Xbox, ordering food, unable to leave the house for over a year, or a young woman who spent nine months in her bedroom after being bullied.

The second includes young people who are not far from work but are locked out of employment by barriers such as having missed a single maths or English grade. And the final category includes youngsters who are ready for work but are suffering due to a lack of accessible jobs

The report adds: “Employers do not reply. Entry-level jobs ask for experience. Apprenticeships are oversubscribed or too far away. Recruitment processes are inaccessible, impersonal or needlessly complex. Over time, repeated rejection starts to look like personal failure, even when it is system failure.”

Article continues below

Mr Hyman said: “This generation is different. Covid plus poverty plus social media plus lack of work experience plus loneliness means getting a job really is difficult. We are letting a generation down.”

Mr Gamote: “The young people we met were not lazy, hopeless or lacking ambition. They were exhausted by a system that made them feel rejected before adult life had even begun.

"Again and again, we met young people who wanted to work and contribute, but were being pushed from one closed door to another. What struck me most was not just the pain young people were carrying, but their resilience. The question is whether Britain is prepared to try as hard for them.”

News.title: ALAN MILBURN: 'Young people are not lazy, distracted or entitled - we must not give up on them'
News.content:
EXCLUSIVE: ALAN MILBURN: 'Young people are not lazy, distracted or entitled - we must not give up on them'

Alan Milburn, a former Labour Health Secretary, talks about what he has uncovered while writing his major review into Britain's youth unemployment crisis

View 3 Images Ex-Health Secretary Alan Milburn says we must not give up on young people

A young person told our Review that applying for work felt like shouting into a void.

‌



Dozens of applications. No reply. Automated rejections. Entry level jobs asking for experience they had never been given the chance to get.

‌



They wanted to work. They wanted a routine. They wanted to earn their own money and build a life. But every door seemed to close before anyone had even looked them in the eye. That story is not unusual. It is the experience of too many young people in Britain today.

‌



Nearly one million young people in the UK are not in education, employment or training. One in eight. A country cannot complain about labour shortages, low growth and rising welfare bills while allowing the talent of nearly one million young people to go to waste.

That should shame us. Not because young people lack talent. Not because they lack ambition. But because too many have been left without a proper route into work, confidence and independence.

Sick notes will no longer be issued to some patients in pilot shaking up 'broken' system READ MORE :

Major drive to get under 25s on benefits into work as businesses offered £3,000 READ MORE :

View 3 Images 'A young person told our Review that applying for work felt like shouting into a void' (Image: Getty Images)

‌



The easy answer is to blame young people. To say they are lazy, distracted or entitled. I do not buy it. As part of my Review, I asked Peter Hyman and Shuab Gamote to listen to young people across the country. Not to lecture them. Not to judge them. But to understand what their lives are really like. What they found should make us think again.

There is no shortage of talent or drive. One young person was teaching herself Russian on Duolingo. Another had set up a TikTok business. A third wanted to coach sport and give back to her community. These are not young people who have checked out. They are resilient, thoughtful and bursting with potential.

But they are growing up in circumstances previous generations did not face all at once. A pandemic that shut them away during formative years. Social media designed to hold their attention. A housing market that feels beyond reach. A jobs market that asks for experience before offering anyone the chance to gain it.

‌



View 3 Images 'Dozens of applications. No reply. Automated rejections. Entry level jobs asking for experience they had never been given the chance to get' (Image: PA)

None of these pressures is completely new on its own. What is new is the combination. And it is landing on young people at the very moment they are trying to move from childhood into adult life.

Yet too often their behaviour is tracked, polled, debated and judged by people who have never asked them what their lives are actually like. They are called lazy, distracted, entitled.

‌



They are not. Every generation is different from the one before it. The question is not whether young people have changed. Of course they have. The question is whether the systems around them have changed too. This time, they have not.

Education has not kept pace with the changing needs of young people or employers. The NHS is still too slow to respond to the mental health and other health challenges that stop young people fully participating. And the welfare system, which should help young people at a crucial moment in life, too often manages people outside work rather than helping them take the first step in.

That has to change. The answer is not to write young people off. Nor is it to pretend that ambition alone can overcome every barrier. The answer is to build a system that starts with what young people can do, not just what they cannot.

Article continues below

That means better routes from school into work. Stronger technical and vocational options. Proper work experience. Earlier mental health support. Employers opening more doors. And welfare support that helps young people try work without fear that one failed step will leave them worse off.

Young people have told us what they want. A chance to get a good job. A chance to build a life. A chance to fulfil their potential. They have not given up on work. We must not give up on them.

News.title: 'Nigel Farage has built an entire career on finding outsiders to blame - this is political scaremongering'
News.content:
'Nigel Farage has built an entire career on finding outsiders to blame - this is political scaremongering'

'Reform UK has poisoned Britain's immigration debate by feeding voters a steay diet of fear, distortion and selective facts'

View Image Voice of the Mirror has its say...

Nigel preys on our fear

Nigel Farage and Reform UK are poisoning Britain’s immigration debate by feeding voters a steady diet of fear, ­distortion and selective facts.

‌



The figures are clear. Net migration has collapsed from 900,000 in 2023 to 204,000 in the year to June 2025 and is projected to fall even further.

‌



Yet almost half the country wrongly believes it is still rising. That is the direct result of years of political scaremongering. Farage has built an entire career on finding outsiders to blame.

‌



First Eastern Europeans. Now migrants crossing the Channel. Targets change but the playbook remains the same. The hypocrisy reeks. He helped drag Britain into Brexit pledging stronger borders, despite leaving the UK outside European return arrangements that tackled asylum claims. The disorder he exploits for applause was fuelled by the project he mis-sold to the public.

More is needed

Any help with the cost of living will be welcomed by families battered by Donald Trump’s reckless war with Iran, years of rising bills and endless economic shocks.

‌



Rachel Reeves is right to act before pressures deepen further. Tariff cuts on daily essentials, freezing fuel duty and helping children travel for free are sensible steps in the right direction.

But nobody should pretend this goes far enough. Millions remain terrified about what lies ahead as energy bills threaten to surge again later this year, while mortgage costs and rents remain painfully high.

The Chancellor is right to move early, but if the government truly wants to shield working people from another brutal winter, bigger intervention will soon be needed.

Article continues below

It takes trio

Strictly Come Dancing has always thrived on fearless reinvention.

The BBC believe Emma Willis, Johannes Radebe and Josh Widdicombe can deliver, and Shirley Ballas clearly thinks Saturday nights will remain cha-cha-charming in their hands.

News.title: Damning report says most voters don't know truth on migration and singles out Nigel Farage
News.content:
Damning report says most voters don't know truth on migration and singles out Nigel Farage

A new report by think-tank British Future points out that net migration has fallen massively, but most voters think it is going up - and accused Nigel Farage of false claims

View 2 Images The report accuses Nigel Farage of trying to undermine data showing net migration is falling (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

Nigel Farage has been accused of spreading misinformation about immigration, with alarming data showing the public wrongly believe it is rising.

‌



Politicians have been blamed for skewing the public's understanding of immigration levels - with Mr Farage accused of trying to undermine the falling number of people arriving.

‌



New research reveals 49% of people believe net migration - the difference between people settling in and leaving the UK - rose in the past year.

‌



In fact it saw a sharp decline, dropping from 900,000 in 2023 to 204,000 in the year to June 2025. But despite the figure being projected to fall below 100,000 by the end of this year, most people expect it to rise.

A report by think-tank British Future claims Mr Farage made false claims about Brits leaving to try and explain the drop. Director Sunder Katwala said: “A massive perception gap is shaping not just the immigration debate but British politics more broadly.

Politicians need to take responsibility for this. It’s little wonder voters think net migration is going up when the only debate we have is about how to bring it down. We should be having a conversation about how to manage the pressures and gains of migration to Britain."

‌



Government will NOT force supermarkets to cap prices of basic foods despite reports, minister insists READ MORE :

View 2 Images Voters have a skewed impression about the number of asylum claims, the data shows (Image: Dan Kitwood/Getty Images)

He called on ministers to publish a yearly immigration plan, stating: "That kind of accountability could take some of the heat out of our immigration debate – and keep the public better informed, too.”

The report claims Reform reacted to Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures showing plummeting net migration by making false claims. It says: "Reform UK has an immigration policy targeting ‘net zero’ immigration but reacted to the November 2025 ONS figures by seeking to undermine the data, with Nigel Farage falsely claiming that the fall in net migration was largely driven by British emigration."

‌



It said a 440,000 annual reduction in net migration was due to a 400,000 fall in new arrivals. But it said Reform is the most trusted party among immigration-sceptics.

The annual Immigration Attitudes Tracker found just 16% of the public correctly think net migration - which includes legal and illegal migration - fell last year. And most believe asylum makes up a third of all immigration, when the true figure is 9%. More than half of immigration into the UK is for study, while nearly a third is for work.

The data showed people who want immigration to fall are most likely to wrongly think it is rising. But just 15% of them think it will actually be achieved in the next year.

Article continues below

The survey of more than 3,000 adults also found most people thinks immigration for study accounts for around a quarter of people coming to live in the UK. In reality it is 52%.

And they also underestimate the proportion coming to the UK to work, which is 31%. The report states: "There is a clear correlation between misperception of net migration numbers and immigration attitudes, including support for reductions and for the political parties promising them.

"Those who feel most negatively about immigration are most likely to mistakenly believe that it increased over the last year and will increase again next year." The Mirror has contacted Reform UK for comment.

News.title: Influencer accused of 'plotting with dad to hire dark web hitman and have boy band singer ex killed'
News.content:
Influencer accused of 'plotting with dad to hire dark web hitman and have boy band singer ex killed'

TikTok star Gabriela Gonzalez is accused of hatching a plot with her lawyer father to murder her pop singer ex-boyfriend Jack Avery by hiring a dark web hitman

View 4 Images Gabriela Gonzalez, 25, is accused of conspiracy to murder (Image: Jam Press)

An influencer and her lawyer dad have been arrested over an alleged plot to hire a dark web hitman and have her boy band singer ex-boyfriend killed.

‌



TikTok star Gabriela Gonzalez is accused by County of Los Angeles prosecutors of conspiring with her dad Francisco, who is an attorney, to arrange the murder of her ex, Jack Avery.

‌



The 25-year-old - who goes by the username gabbieegonzalez on TikTok and is known for her lifestyle, travel and motherhood content - has a seven-year-old daughter with her ex-boyfriend, according to a police report.

‌



Mr Avery, 26, is a former member of the boy band Why Don’t We, whose 2018 debut studio album '8 Letters' peaked at number 9 in the US album charts, and number 28 in the UK.

View 4 Images Jack Avery is a former singer with the boy band Why Don’t We (Image: Jam Press)

A police report quoted by LA district attorneys said the couple have been locked in a "longstanding custody and visitation" battle, which Gabbie's dad is said to be "deeply involved" in.

‌



Francisco Gonzalez is alleged to have hired a private investigator to spy on Jack, including looking for evidence that he was drinking, smoking, or "acting in a way that could be used against him in the custody dispute." In one incident, he is said to have threatened to have Mr Avery arrested if he showed up to visit his daughter.

View 4 Images Dad Francisco Javier Gonzalez is said to have driven the plot to find a dark web hitman (Image: Jam Press)

Prosecutors allege that between 2020 and 2021, Gabriela asked her then-boyfriend, Kai Cordrey, to help her find a hitman over the dark web to kill Jack.

‌



Her dad sent Cordrey a $10,000 (£7,400) payment to assist in the task, which he wrote off as a fee for a web development task, they said. Cordrey asked for another $4,000 (£2,900), which Francisco is alleged to have paid.

In September 2021, Codrey is alleged to have began communicating with undercover law enforcement agent posing as a hitman, reportedly telling him that Mr Avery was the target, discussing method of payment and asking how death would be proved.

Cordrey allegedly went on to tell the hitman that Gabriela Gonzalez had ordered the murder and that Francisco would stump up the money.

Article continues below

View 4 Images Gonzalez faces a maximum life sentence if convicted (Image: Jam Press)

Gabriela was arrested last week in California, while her dad was detained in Lake Mary, Florida on Monday over conspiracy to commit murder, solicitation of murder, and attempted murder-for-hire. They and Codrey were officially charged on Tuesrday,

The trio face a maximum sentence of 25 years to life if convicted, according to state officials. Jack Avery filed a restraining order against his ex-girlfriend after news of her arrest emerged, reported TMZ.

News.title: Southampton lose appeal against play-off expulsion
News.content:
Southampton's appeal against being thrown out of the Championship play-off final for spying has been rejected.

The match will now go ahead on Saturday between Hull City and Middlesbrough (15:30 BST kick-off), with a place in the Premier League on the line.

An EFL independent disciplinary commission on Tuesday evening expelled Southampton from the play-offs and reinstated Middlesbrough, who had lost 2-1 to the Saints on aggregate in the semi-finals.

Southampton appealed against their removal, calling it "manifestly disproportionate to every previous sanction in the history of the English game". However, the EPL has rejected Saints' appeal and upheld the punishment.

"A league arbitration panel has tonight dismissed Southampton Football Club's appeal against the independent disciplinary commission's sanction following the admittance of multiple breaches of EFL regulations," the EFL said on Wednesday.

"The determination means that the original sanction of expulsion from the Championship play-offs remains in place, as does the four-point deduction to be applied to the 2026-27 Championship table and the reprimand in respect of all charges."

The decision is final and there is no further right of appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport.

Southampton issued a statement calling the ruling "an extremely disappointing outcome".

It added: "While we fully acknowledge the seriousness of this matter and the scrutiny that has followed, the club has consistently believed the original sporting sanction was disproportionate, a view that has been widely shared by many in the football community over the last 24 hours.

"While tonight is a painful moment, this football club will respond with humility, accountability and determination to put things right."

Saints midfielder Leo Scienza said his side's expulsion was "heartbreaking" and expressed sympathy for everyone involved, including Hull and Middlesbrough.

He posted on Instagram, external: "Disappointment, anger, sadness. It's difficult to find the right words for what we're all feeling right now.

"What has happened over the last days is heartbreaking. For the club, for every player in this dressing room, and above all for our supporters. A moment like this should never end the way it did.

"I feel sorry for every football fan, as well as the players and supporters of Hull and Boro, who were caught up in all of this chaos too.

"We gave everything for this dream. Day after day, sacrifice after sacrifice, always believing we could bring this club back to where it belongs. For me, the dream of playing in the Premier League was something I fought for with everything I had. That's why this pain cuts so deep."

News.content:

A real estate broker says an organization denied her the opportunity to purchase land in an Arkansas development because of her Jewish ancestry, and because she has a Black husband and biracial children, according to a lawsuit filed Wednesday in federal court.

The lawsuit, filed in Arkansas on behalf of Michelle Walker, names Return to the Land, a development whose owners have said they must personally confirm that applicants are white before they are accepted, its Ozarks chapter and five officers. It says Return to the Land founders are “explicitly attempting to establish an all-white community.”

The lawsuit also calls Return to the Land a white nationalist organization and says it's in violation of federal and state fair housing and civil rights acts.

“Its founders believe that white people are genetically superior to other races, advance the view that Jewish people are engaged in a plot to eliminate the white race, and advocate for segregated white communities for the purpose of creating a separate all-white nation state that will help avoid ‘white genocide,’” the lawsuit said.

For decades, Blacks and other minorities were restricted from buying or renting homes in some neighborhoods or areas due to racial covenants built into mortgages and leases. Prospective homebuyers also faced redlining in which mortgages and loans were denied based on race.

Walker, a real estate broker who lives in St. Louis, applied to buy land last year in the town of Ravenden, Arkansas, due to its below-market price. Ravenden is about 150 miles (241 kilometers) northeast of Little Rock and just south of the state line with Missouri.

She was asked questions during the application process about her ancestry, religion and her family, according to the lawsuit.

Walker is white and belongs to a Christian church. Her Jewish ancestry is on her mother's side.

She is represented in the lawsuit by the Relman Colfax law firm, the Legal Defense Fund, and Legal Aid of Arkansas.

Return to the Land did not respond to an email Wednesday from The Associated Press seeking comment on the lawsuit.

On its website, Return to the Land promotes itself as a private membership association “for individuals and families with traditional views and common continental ancestry." In addition to the its Ozarks Regional Chapter which covers parts of Arkansas, Missouri and eastern Oklahoma, Return to the Land says it has chapters around the United States.

After reports that Return to the Land was eyeing the Springfield, Missouri-area for a whites-only community, Springfield’s city council said in a Facebook post last July that there was no place in the city “or anywhere, for such a divisive and discriminatory vision.”

Pennsylvania’s state House in April passed — by a ultra-slim vote of 101-100 — a bill to block the creation of whites-only housing communities. House Bill 2103 followed Return to the Land’s believed intention to expand to Pennsylvania and other states.

The legislation now is before the Pennsylvania Senate.

____

Williams is a member of The Associated Press Race & Ethnicities team. He reported from Detroit.

Six Flags Over Texas will open a new roller coaster this year designed to claim six world records, including the titles for the tallest, fastest and longest dive coaster.

The ride, named Tormenta Rampaging Run, is scheduled to debut in 2026 at the theme park in Arlington, Texas. The flagship park is one of two major Six Flags theme parks in the state.

The attraction will be located within a newly designed Spanish-themed area of the park called Rancho de la Tormenta, though an official opening date has not yet been confirmed.

According to specifications released by Six Flags, the coaster will climb to a peak of 309 feet before releasing riders into a 285-foot drop. That descent will plunge at a 95-degree angle, tilting past a standard vertical drop. The ride is engineered to reach a top speed of 87 miles per hour across 4,199 feet of track.

The park confirmed the coaster will also feature a 218-foot Immelmann inversion — a maneuver that flips riders upside down before tracking them in the opposite direction — and a 179-foot vertical loop, both expected to set industry records.

The ride will serve as the anchor for Rancho de la Tormenta, a new Spanish-themed plaza featuring regional music and banners ( Six Flags Over Texas )

The park claims the ride has already smashed six world records, including those for tallest, longest, and fastest dive coaster, and for the highest drop with inversion.

To board, passengers must meet a minimum height requirement of 48 inches, or 4 ft tall, with a maximum restriction capped at 76 inches, or 6ft 3 inches.

The ride’s design anchors a new, heavily themed Spanish plaza within the park called Rancho de la Tormenta. Park officials said the area will feature regional music and banners, and the open-air coaster trains will be styled to evoke the traditional attire worn during the Running of the Bulls.

The announcement comes as amusement parks across the country ramp up investment in record-breaking rides to attract travelers. Major competitors are rolling out similar anchor attractions this summer, including a drifting coaster themed around the “Fast & Furious” film franchise at Universal Studios Hollywood.

Six Flags has not yet disclosed an exact opening date for the Texas coaster, stating only that it will debut later this year.

A fascinating glimpse into maritime superstition has emerged from HMS Victory, as six 19th-century coins and tokens were unearthed beneath the warship's foremast.

The discovery came during the latest phase of a decade-long, £42 million restoration, which saw a 750-tonne crane meticulously remove the mizzen, foremast, and bowsprit from Vice-Admiral Lord Nelson’s iconic flagship at Portsmouth Historic Dockyard.

Conservationists made the find after the masts were lifted, revealing the coins, which were traditionally placed there to bestow good fortune upon the vessel and its crew.

Andrew Baines, executive director of museum operations at Royal Navy Museums, said: “We are incredibly excited to have discovered six coins beneath the fore lower mast of HMS Victory. This find connects us directly to a maritime tradition stretching back thousands of years.

“The placing of coins beneath a ship’s mast has long been seen as a symbolic act, often associated with protection and good fortune for the vessel and her crew.

open image in gallery After their removal, conservationists found the coins which had been placed under the foremast as part of a tradition to bring good fortune to the vessel and crew ( PA )

“Following the earlier discovery of a single farthing beneath the main lower mast, we had hoped there might be something similar beneath the foremast. But to uncover six coins was an extraordinary surprise.”

Five of the coins date to the period when the foremast was stepped in 1894, when the ship’s original wooden masts were replaced with wrought iron versions.

The sixth coin has been identified as a token from Prince Edward Island, Canada, dated to 1835 with an image of a ship stamped on it.

Mr Baines said: “The 1835 Prince Edward Island token is one of the most intriguing finds. Its inscription, ‘Ships, Colonies and Commerce’ – a slogan closely associated with the maritime and imperial trade networks of the 19th century – reflects the world in which HMS Victory served and suggests these coins may have been chosen for symbolic as well as practical reasons.

“We cannot yet say why this particular token was selected, but its presence beneath the foremast adds another layer to the story.

open image in gallery One of the coins has been identified as a token from Prince Edward Island, Canada, dated to 1835 ( Collective Wisdom )

“Hidden from view for more than a century, these objects nevertheless speak directly to the people who cared for Victory and the traditions they chose to continue.”

Karoline Sofie Hennum, conservator on HMS Victory, said that all of the coins had been heavily degraded from the prolonged pressure of the 50 tonnes of mast, along with corrosion from the 132 years since they were placed there.

She said: “To unlock the secrets of the coins covered up by decades of corrosion, they needed to be removed from the base plate, cleaned and X-rayed.

“Luckily, overall, the condition of the coins was good, and they came away from the base easily.

“Then using a microscope, we carefully cleaned them with brushes, wooden skewers and tweezers, bringing more information to light.

“Finally, using a technique called X-radiography, we could see beneath the corrosion revealing both sides of the coin in one image.”

The five coins are three one penny pieces featuring a “bun head” portrait of Queen Victoria, two of which dated to 1890 and one to 1892, with a halfpenny dated to 1890, along with a farthing dated to 1882.

They will go on display from May 23 in the Victory Gallery at Portsmouth Historic Dockyard.

HMS Victory, which is the world’s oldest commissioned warship, was Nelson’s flagship at the Battle of Trafalgar and it was on the ship’s quarterdeck that he was fatally shot by a French sniper on October 21 1805.

Victory was first floated out at Chatham in 1765 but by the 1920s was in poor condition and moved to dry dock in Portsmouth, Hampshire, in 1922.

A scaffolding structure will now enclose the ship and remain in place until the conservation work is completed in 2033.

Three people have died and more than a dozen first responders have been hospitalized following a possible hazmat situation in New Mexico.

At around 11:00 a.m., local time Wednesday, New Mexico State Police rushed to a home in Mountainair for a “suspected overdose,” according to authorities.

Four people inside the home were found “unresponsive,” and three of them have since been confirmed dead, the state police said in a Facebook post.

Eighteen first responders were exposed to an “unidentified substance” and taken to the hospital along with the other person inside the home, authorities said. Several first responders have since been released.

The first responders experienced symptoms including nausea and dizziness, after being exposed to the substance, according to state police. Two of them were in serious condition as of Wednesday afternoon.

open image in gallery Three people have died and more than a dozen first responders have been hospitalized following a possible hazmat situation in New Mexico ( Google Earth )

At least one person inside the home was revived with Narcan, Torrance County Sheriff David Frazee said in an article published by the Santa Fe New Mexican. Narcan is used to try to save people suspected of overdosing on an opioid.

"Evidently, they must have inhaled some toxins or something from the scene," Frazee said of the first responders.

Mountainair Mayor Peter Nieto said the first responders had “direct contact with the individual who passed, and they were feeling lightheaded, headaches, nausea, things like that,” per the Santa Fe New Mexican.

Nieto said in a Facebook post that while the exact cause of the incident is currently unknown, “all indications are pointing toward narcotics as a possible factor.”

The first responders and the one person inside the home who was still alive were taken to the University of New Mexico Hospital. They are being “quarantined, evaluated, and monitored,” state police said.

New Mexico State Police arrived at the home to help the Torrance County Sheriff’s Office. It’s unclear how many members of each agency were affected by the unknown substance.

Three of the four EMTs from Mountainair EMS have been released from the hospital, Nieto said in a follow-up Facebook post.

EMS Chief Josh Lewis, who was the first to enter the home, will remain in the hospital overnight for observation, the mayor said.

“We are incredibly thankful that the other responders have been released,” Nieto said. “While they are not yet fully recovered, they are doing much better.”

open image in gallery At least one person inside the home was revived with Narcan, Torrance County Sheriff David Frazee said ( AFP via Getty Images )

Some Torrance County EMTs and hospital nurses who came into contact with people who were at the home also experienced symptoms, according to the mayor.

“We are keeping them in our thoughts and prayers and wishing them a full and speedy recovery,” Nieto said.

Albuquerque Fire Rescue Hazmat teams are working to identify the substance. Investigators believe it may be spread through contact rather than being airborne, according to authorities.

Mountainair Public Works confirmed that the substance was not carbon monoxide or related to natural gas.

Authorities said they secured a perimeter around the home and that there is “no threat to the public.”

“We ask the public to avoid the area and keep all affected individuals and first responders in their thoughts,” state police said.

Nieto also responded to what he said were “comments claiming that we are not taking the drug situation seriously.”

“We absolutely are,” the mayor said. “Our first responders, law enforcement, medical personnel, and local officials work every day to protect this community and respond to difficult situations.”
